title: The Data Science Lifecycle
blurb: Tests whether you can tell which lifecycle stage a project is really in, spot how it is failing, and judge when it may move on or must loop back.

questions.prompt: Which of this book's eight lifecycle stages has **no explicit phase** in CRISP-DM?
options: Business understanding (problem framing)
Evaluation
Monitoring
Data preparation
questions.explanation: CRISP-DM runs business understanding, data understanding, data preparation, modelling, evaluation and deployment. It stops there. Monitoring is "(not explicit)" in the Framework Comparison. TDSP adds it as ongoing deployment and customer acceptance. Evaluation is a tempting pick because TDSP folds it into Modeling, but CRISP-DM names it as its own phase.

refLinks.label: §10.2.1 The Stages, Mapped to This Book

questions.prompt: The chapter says the lifecycle is often confused with a project plan. What does it say the lifecycle is instead?
options: A state machine: the states a project can be in and the moves between them
A schedule: a fixed sequence of stages, each with its own delivery date
A gated waterfall: each stage must be signed off before the next may start
A pipeline with a single feedback arrow from monitoring back to framing
questions.explanation: The lifecycle is a project state machine. Every stage has an edge back to every earlier stage. That is why two projects on the same lifecycle can take a week or a year. The single-feedback-arrow picture is exactly the textbook diagram the chapter says lies.

questions.prompt: Which failure mode does the chapter call the **most common** in industry?
options: Data leakage goes undetected until production, when the leaked feature no longer exists
The model is evaluated once, on one static test set, and never re-evaluated
Nobody asks whether ML is the right tool, so months go on a problem SQL would solve
It works in the notebook, but nobody built the serving path to production
questions.explanation: Deployment is the stage most projects never reach. Industry surveys find most prototypes never make it to production. The other three are real failure modes from the table, attached to data preparation, evaluation and problem framing. The chapter does not rank them as most common.

refLinks.label: §10.2.3 Why Projects Die at Each Stage

questions.prompt: According to the Stage Checklist, what is the exit criterion for **stage 5, Evaluation**?
options: The model's AUC-ROC is clearly above 0.5 on the held-out test set
The model is reachable in production and a rollback plan exists
Model metric and business metric both meet the stage-1 thresholds
At least one trained candidate model beats the baseline
questions.explanation: Evaluation exits only when both the model metric and the business metric clear the thresholds signed off in stage 1. "Beats the baseline" is the stage 4 (modelling) exit, a lower bar. "Reachable in production with a rollback plan" is the stage 6 exit.

questions.prompt: In the Decision Guide, a stakeholder wants predictions, a simple rule does not suffice, and **no historical labelled data exists**. What is the triage outcome?
options: A full lifecycle project, using the charter template
Ship a simple rule, since no ML model can be trained
Data collection project first, revisit once labels exist
An EDA/analytics task rather than a lifecycle project
questions.explanation: Without labels there is nothing to train a supervised model against. The next step is to build a labelling or data collection process. Shipping a rule is wrong here because the guide has already established that a simple rule does not meet the required performance.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter warn against skipping **kill criteria** in the project charter?
options: Auditors need them before they will approve a CRISP-DM process
Kill criteria are needed to decide the train/test split ratio
Without an exit condition, projects tend to survive on sunk cost
Without them the monitoring owner does not know when to page anyone
questions.explanation: Kill criteria state in advance when the project is cancelled rather than continued, for example "baseline doesn't beat the existing rule by 10%". Without one, a doomed project keeps consuming months because nobody has a trigger to stop it. Paging is the job of the named monitoring owner, a different charter field.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, a `DummyClassifier(strategy='most_frequent')` is fitted to churn data with a 7% churn rate. What does it score on the positive (churn) class?
options: Recall 0.00, since it never predicts churn
Recall 0.50, because it guesses at random
Recall 0.07, because 7% of customers churn
Recall 0.93, the same as its accuracy
questions.explanation: `most_frequent` always predicts the majority class, "no churn". It scores 93% accuracy and catches zero churners, so precision and recall on the positive class are both 0.00. The 93% figure is accuracy, not recall. This is the chapter's example of why accuracy is the wrong metric on imbalanced data.

questions.prompt: A retail customer's team is pulling order history from S3 and discovers that the `returned` label was only recorded from March onwards, after a system migration. Which lifecycle stage are they in when they find this?
options: Stage 7, monitoring for drift
Stage 3, data preparation and cleaning
Stage 2, data understanding
Stage 5, evaluation of the label
questions.explanation: Stage 2 is where the team identifies sources, pulls data and documents its quality, coverage and limitations. A label that only exists for part of the window is a coverage and label-reliability finding, which is stage 2's exit criterion. Data preparation (stage 3) is tempting because a fix may happen there, but the discovery itself is understanding, not transformation.

refLinks.label: §10.2.1 The Stages, Mapped to This Book

questions.prompt: A fraud model reaches AUC 0.88 and the team celebrates. The business owner then explains that investigators can only review the top 200 alerts per day, and what matters is precision on those 200. Nobody optimised for that. Where should the project loop back to?
options: Stage 2, to collect more fraud examples before anything else
Stage 6, to deploy now and adjust the threshold in production
Stage 1, to redefine success as precision at 200 alerts per day
Stage 4, to tune hyperparameters until the AUC is higher still
questions.explanation: This is the chapter's evaluation loop-back. Stage 5 has revealed that the success metric itself was wrong. The fix is to rewrite the stage-1 definition of success, then re-evaluate against it. Tuning for more AUC is the tempting move, but it optimises a metric the business does not use.

questions.prompt: During data preparation, a candidate feature `days_since_cancellation_call` correlates at 0.94 with the churn label. Which failure mode is this the early warning sign for?
options: Label drift: the churn definition changed within the historical window
Optimising the wrong metric: the model metric will not map to the business metric
Redundancy: the feature duplicates another predictor and should be dropped for collinearity
Leakage: the feature is probably not available at prediction time
questions.explanation: The Common Failure Modes table lists "suspiciously high correlation with label (> 0.9)" as the warning sign for leakage in data preparation. A cancellation call happens as part of churning, so the feature would not exist when the model has to score a still-active customer. Redundancy is about two features correlating with each other, not a feature with the label.

refLinks.label: §10.2.3 Why Projects Die at Each Stage

questions.prompt: Select ALL items that are part of the **stage 6, Deployment** exit criteria in the Stage Checklist.
options: The business metric is moving
The model is reachable in production
A named owner receives alerts
A retraining trigger is defined
A rollback plan exists
questions.explanation: Deployment exits when the model is reachable in production and a rollback plan exists. A named alert owner and a retraining trigger are the stage 7 (monitoring) exit criteria. "Business metric moving" belongs to the charter's definition of done for the whole project, not to one stage.

questions.prompt: A finance stakeholder asks for "an ML model" that flags every invoice above £10,000 for manual approval. Using Procedure 10.3, what is the right triage outcome?
options: Full lifecycle project: write a charter
Not a project: write the rule and ship it
Data collection first: gather labelled approvals
Run a 1-day EDA spike before committing
questions.explanation: The requirement is a fixed threshold. A one-line rule meets it exactly, so the first branch applies: "write the rule, ship it in a day". The full-lifecycle answer is tempting because the stakeholder said "ML model", but the triage asks what the problem needs, not what the requester named.

questions.prompt: A charter's kill criterion reads: "cancel if the model does not beat the existing rule's precision by at least 10% (relative) at the same alert volume". At 400 alerts per month the rule catches 88 real churners. The model, also at 400 alerts, catches 104. What is the model's relative improvement in precision over the rule? Give a percentage to 1 d.p.
questions.explanation: Rule precision $= 88/400 = 0.220$. Model precision $= 104/400 = 0.260$. Relative improvement $= 0.260/0.220 - 1 = 104/88 - 1 = 0.1818$, so **18.2%**. That clears the 10% bar. Note the absolute gain is only 4 percentage points. A charter should say whether "10%" is relative or absolute, because the two readings can disagree.

questions.prompt: A test set holds 1,500 customers with a 6% churn rate. A hand-written rule flags 150 customers with a precision of 12%. What is the rule's recall on churners? Give a decimal to 3 d.p.
questions.explanation: Churners $= 0.06 \times 1500 = 90$. True positives $= 0.12 \times 150 = 18$. Recall $= 18/90 =$ **0.200**. A common slip is dividing by the 150 flagged customers, which gives precision again, not recall.

questions.prompt: A customer's team has trained 14 candidate models over six weeks. Their best reaches AUC 0.91. When you ask what number the business sponsor signed off as "good enough", nobody knows, because the sponsor was never asked. Using the chapter's mental model, which stage is this project in, whatever the activity suggests?
options: Stage 4, modelling, because candidate models are being trained and tuned
Stage 6, deployment, because the model has beaten any reasonable baseline
Stage 5, evaluation, because a strong held-out AUC exists
Stage 1, problem framing, because no success metric has been agreed
questions.explanation: The mental model says it directly. If the metrics look great but nobody agreed what "great" means for the business, the project is still in stage 1, no matter how much modelling code exists. Stage 1's exit criterion (success metric signed off) was never met. Stage 4 is the tempting answer because that is where the activity is, but the skill the chapter asks for is knowing which stage you are in versus the one you think you are in.

questions.prompt: A customer wants a churn model. Their programme office insists on a 40-page requirements specification, signed by six stakeholders, before anyone is given data access. Which advice best fits the chapter's framing trade-off?
options: Skip framing and start modelling, since the data will define the problem anyway
Follow CRISP-DM literally so each phase is cleared as a gate before the next starts
Write a lightweight problem statement, do a fast EDA pass, then revise the statement
Treat it as an Elephant project, since six stakeholders need a complete formal specification
questions.explanation: Nobody can know what is realistic until the data has been seen. The chapter recommends a quick Chapter 2 statement, a fast EDA pass and a revised statement: iterate the contract. Data science projects should be treated as Rabbits. The Elephant option is tempting because of the stakeholder count, but writing an Elephant's specification for a project the data will reshape within a week is the named failure mode. Skipping framing entirely is the opposite error.

questions.prompt: A churn model went live eight months ago via a nightly batch job. Its precision has since fallen from 0.42 to 0.18. The team noticed only when finance asked why the retention campaign's return had dropped. Drift alerts were routed to a shared inbox nobody reads, and the model was never re-scored against fresh labelled data. Select ALL failure modes this evidence supports.
options: Deployment: the model never left the notebook
Problem framing: ML was used where a simple rule would do
Evaluation: a one-off evaluation that was never repeated
Monitoring: no one owns production health
questions.explanation: Alerts routed to an unread inbox is the monitoring warning sign: nobody owns production health. Never re-scoring against fresh data is the evaluation failure, "evaluated once... silent staleness". Deployment did happen, since a nightly batch job ran for eight months. Nothing in the evidence says a rule would have sufficed, so that option is unsupported.

refLinks.label: §10.2.3 Why Projects Die at Each Stage

questions.prompt: In the worked example, the logistic regression reaches AUC-ROC $\approx 0.638$ and beats both baselines. At the threshold that gives recall $\geq 0.60$, its precision is about 0.103, against a stage-1 target of precision $\geq 0.40$. Which statement about the exit criteria is correct?
options: Both are met, since beating the existing rule is the business metric
Stage 5's exit is met, since the AUC is well above random guessing
Stage 4's exit is not met because the model misses the precision target
Stage 4's exit is met but stage 5's is not. Loop back to stage 3 or 1
questions.explanation: Stage 4 only requires that at least one model beats the baseline, and it does. Stage 5 requires that the model metric and business metric both meet the stage-1 thresholds. Precision 0.103 misses 0.40, so stage 5 fails. The chapter's move is to loop back to stage 3 for better features or stage 1 to renegotiate the metric, not to deploy. The AUC option is tempting, but AUC was never the contract.

options: `Not a project -- write the rule, ship it in a day`
`Not a lifecycle project -- this is an analytics/EDA task`
`Unclear -- run a 1-day spike using EDA`
`Not ready -- this is a data collection project first`
questions.explanation: The checks run in order and return at the first match. `simple_rule_suffices` is False, so it moves on. `not historical_labelled_data_exists` is True, so it returns "Not ready -- data collection" before it ever reads `one_off_analysis_only`. The EDA answer is what the stakeholder needs, since a descriptive analysis does not need labels. That gap is a limit of the check order in the listing, and a reason to read triage output with judgement.

questions.prompt: Nine months into a demand-forecasting project, the team is still tuning models in notebooks. Nothing has been deployed, and nobody has proposed stopping. Select ALL charter elements from Listing 10.1 whose absence most directly explains this.
options: A named owner for the serving path (deployment)
A pinned `requirements.txt`
Kill criteria stating when the project is cancelled
A `data/raw/` folder that is never modified
A go/no-go decision date on the timeline
questions.explanation: No kill criteria means nothing triggers a stop, so sunk cost wins. No named deployment owner is the early warning sign for "never leaves the notebook". No go/no-go date means no forced decision point. The read-only raw folder and pinned requirements are good repository hygiene from Procedure 10.4, but they are not charter fields and do not explain a stalled project.
questions.ref: Procedure 10.1, Quick Reference: Common Failure Modes

questions.prompt: A churn test set has 2,000 customers and a 6% churn rate. The stage-1 contract is precision $\geq 0.40$ at recall $\geq 0.60$. At the threshold where recall first reaches 0.65, the model flags 500 customers. What is its precision at that threshold? Give a decimal to 3 d.p.
questions.explanation: Churners $= 0.06 \times 2000 = 120$. True positives $= 0.65 \times 120 = 78$. Precision $= 78/500 =$ **0.156**. The recall target is met, but precision is well short of 0.40. As in the worked example, the model fails the contract and should loop back rather than ship.

questions.prompt: Monitoring on a deployed churn model shows the predicted-churn rate jumping from 7% to 12% overnight. The data team explains that the billing system now records a plan downgrade as `churned = 1`. What response best follows the chapter?
options: Close the alert as a data issue, since the model code is unchanged
Treat it as a new problem statement and revisit the label in stages 1 and 2
Raise the decision threshold until the flagged rate returns to 7%
Retrain immediately on the last three months so the model learns the new label definition
questions.explanation: Well-run teams treat monitoring alerts as new problem statements, not tickets to patch. A label that changed definition is the data-understanding failure mode ("label definition changed within the historical window"). Whether downgrades should count as churn is a business question for stage 1. Retraining is the tempting quick fix, but it trains on a label with two meanings and bakes in a definition nobody signed off. Moving the threshold hides the symptom.

questions.prompt: A churn model scored AUC 0.97 offline. In its first week in production, precision collapses. Investigation shows that the top feature, `retention_offer_sent`, is only written to the warehouse after an agent handles a cancellation request. Which diagnosis is correct?
options: Leakage slipped past stage 3. Rebuild features from data known at prediction time
Stage 1 failed. The success metric was wrong, so renegotiate the target
Stage 7 failed. Production data has drifted, so retrain on the latest month
Stage 6 failed. Serving computes features unlike the notebook, so fix the job
questions.explanation: The feature is recorded after the outcome it predicts. That is leakage from data preparation: the leaked feature does not exist at prediction time. The 0.97 offline AUC was the warning sign. Retraining on recent data (the drift answer) would keep the leaked feature and fail again. A serving-path bug is plausible in general, but here the root cause is the feature's timing, not its computation.

refLinks.label: §10.2.3 Why Projects Die at Each Stage

questions.prompt: Same test set as before: 2,000 customers, 6% churn, contract precision $\geq 0.40$ at recall $\geq 0.60$. To meet the contract exactly at recall 0.60, what is the **maximum** number of customers the model may flag? Give an integer.
questions.explanation: Recall 0.60 of 120 churners means $0.60 \times 120 = 72$ true positives. Precision $\geq 0.40$ means flagged $\leq 72 / 0.40 = 180$. So the model may flag at most **180** customers while catching 72 churners. The model in the previous question flagged 500. This backwards calculation tells the team, and the business owner, how far the model is from the contract in operational terms.

questions.prompt: For the model that flags 500 of the 2,000 customers and catches 78 of the 120 churners, what is its **accuracy**? Give a percentage to 1 d.p.
questions.explanation: TP $= 78$, FP $= 500 - 78 = 422$, FN $= 120 - 78 = 42$, TN $= 1880 - 422 = 1458$. Accuracy $= (78 + 1458)/2000 = 0.768$, so **76.8%**. The always-no-churn dummy scores $1880/2000 = 94.0\%$. The model that finds 65% of churners has lower accuracy than the one that finds none. That is why the stage-1 contract is written in precision and recall, not accuracy.

bookExercises.prompt: Name the eight lifecycle stages in order. For each, name one chapter (or block of chapters) in this book where that stage's skills live.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: 1. Problem framing: Chapter 2. 2. Data collection & understanding: Chapters 7-9. 3. Data preparation: Chapters 7 and 14. 4. Modelling: Chapters 11-20. 5. Evaluation: Chapters 13 and 16. 6. Deployment: the later deployment chapters. 7. Monitoring: the later MLOps/monitoring chapters. 8. Iteration: loops back to Chapter 2's problem framing.

bookExercises.prompt: Explain in two or three sentences why the textbook left-to-right pipeline diagram is misleading, using at least one concrete example of a backward loop from this chapter.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The left-to-right pipeline diagram implies each stage is finished once and handed off to the next, but real projects loop backward constantly: evaluation (stage 5) routinely reveals the success metric itself was wrong. A model hits a strong AUC, the team celebrates, and the business owner then explains they cared about precision at a specific operating point nobody optimised for, sending the project back to stage 1. Similarly, modelling (stage 4) routinely sends a project back to data preparation (stage 3) when a model's errors reveal a feature bug or missing signal. The two stages cycle many times rather than completing in sequence. A diagram with a single feedback arrow tacked on at the end can't represent a process where nearly every stage has an edge back to nearly every earlier one.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 10.3, construct an `ask` dictionary describing a hypothetical stakeholder request where `historical_labelled_data_exists` is `False`. Report what the function returns, and why that's the correct triage outcome.
bookExercises.modelAnswer:
Take this `ask` dictionary:

```python
ask = {
    "simple_rule_suffices": False,
    "historical_labelled_data_exists": False,
    "one_off_analysis_only": False,
    "requires_deployed_prediction_system": True,
}
```

It describes, say, a stakeholder who wants to predict equipment failures but has never logged which equipment failed. It returns `"Not ready -- this is a data collection project first, an ML project second"`. This is the correct outcome because Listing 10.3 checks `simple_rule_suffices` first (false here, so it doesn't short-circuit to "ship a rule"), then checks whether historical labelled data exists. It doesn't, so no amount of modelling skill can produce a supervised model yet. The correct next step is building a labelling/data-collection process, not starting a lifecycle project that has no label to train against.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 10.6' logic as a model, compute what accuracy the naive "predict majority class" baseline would score on a dataset with a 3% positive rate. Explain why that number is a poor argument for using the naive baseline in production.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: On a dataset with a 3% positive rate, the naive "predict majority class" baseline (always predict the negative class) scores **97% accuracy** by construction. It is the negative class's share of the data. That number is a poor argument for production use because the baseline achieves it while catching zero positives. Precision and recall on the positive class are both 0.00. The model is useless for any business action that depends on identifying positives. This is the exact scenario the tutorial's dummy classifier shows at 93% accuracy and 7% churn). A high accuracy figure on an imbalanced dataset says nothing about whether the model does the one thing it's being built for.

bookExercises.prompt: The tutorial's logistic regression achieved AUC-ROC of approximately 0.638 but failed to meet the precision/recall target from Stage 1. Using this chapter's Stage 5 discussion, name the two specific stages the project should loop back to. For each, give one concrete change that might close the gap.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The two stages to loop back to are stage 3 (data preparation) and stage 1 (problem framing/success metric). For stage 3: add richer features. The tutorial notebook works from only six raw features: support tickets, payment failures, login recency, tenure, plan type, product count. Engineering additional signals, such as usage trend over time, interaction-weighted engagement scores, or billing-cycle-relative features (Chapter 14), could give the model more to separate churners from non-churners than a modest AUC of 0.638 suggests is currently available. For stage 1: renegotiate the success metric. Precision $\geq$ 0.40 at recall $\geq$ 0.60 may be unattainable with the signal currently available. The business owner may need to accept a different operating point, such as lower recall in exchange for usable precision. Or they may need a different intervention design, such as a broader, cheaper retention outreach that tolerates lower precision. The alternative is asking the model to hit a target the data can't support yet.

bookExercises.prompt: Rewrite the tutorial's Stage 6 deployment plan for a scenario where the business owner instead wants real-time scoring at the moment a customer contacts support, rather than nightly batch scoring. What changes about the serving pattern, the latency budget, and the rollback plan?
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Moving from nightly batch scoring to real-time scoring at the moment of a support contact changes all three elements the tutorial's Stage 6 plan assumed. The serving pattern shifts from a scheduled batch job over the full customer base to a request-response endpoint invoked synchronously (or near-synchronously) when a support interaction begins. The model needs to be behind a low-latency API, e.g. a SageMaker real-time endpoint, rather than a nightly Batch Transform job. Features need to be computable on demand rather than pre-joined the night before, which likely requires a feature store with fresh, queryable feature values, rather than a batch feature table. The latency budget tightens dramatically. Batch scoring can tolerate minutes to hours per run. A support-interaction-triggered prediction needs to return in well under a second, so it doesn't stall the support agent's workflow. This rules out any model or feature pipeline with expensive real-time joins or slow feature computation. The rollback plan also changes. A bad batch run can be discarded and rerun before anyone sees the output. A bad real-time model is affecting live support decisions immediately. So the rollback plan needs an instant traffic-shifting mechanism, e.g. an endpoint alias or canary rollback, rather than "rerun the job." It also needs a fallback response, such as defaulting to the old rule-based flag, if the real-time endpoint is unavailable or too slow.

bookExercises.prompt: A team tells you they "follow CRISP-DM," but their retrospectives show every project has shipped a model that was never revisited after deployment. Using this chapter's Framework Comparison discussion, explain which stage CRISP-DM under-specifies that likely explains this pattern. Explain what TDSP would have required instead.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: CRISP-DM under-specifies monitoring. Per the Framework Comparison, it has no explicit monitoring phase at all, ending effectively at deployment. A team that "follows CRISP-DM" literally has no process step that requires anyone to watch the model after it ships. No dashboards, no alerts, and critically no named owner for production health. That explains exactly the pattern described: models get shipped and never revisited. TDSP would have required an explicit deployment-as-ongoing / customer-acceptance stage with monitoring dashboards, drift alerts, and, per this chapter's RACI table, a named individual (not "the team") accountable for receiving those alerts and triggering retraining. The gap isn't a modelling failure. It's a process framework that never asked "who watches this after ship day."

bookExercises.prompt: Read the original CRISP-DM paper (Wirth & Hipp, 2000) or the Microsoft TDSP documentation. Compare its treatment of "iteration" to this chapter's Stage 8. Does the source treat iteration as a distinct, named stage with its own deliverable, or as an implicit property of the whole process? What does that difference suggest about how seriously each framework takes the "loop back" problem?
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only, no single answer. Worth examining directly: the original CRISP-DM paper treats deployment as its sixth and final phase, with only a brief note that the process is "cyclic." It offers no dedicated deliverable, checklist, or owner for what an iteration requires. Iteration is a property asserted of the diagram, not a phase with its own exit criteria. TDSP's documentation, by contrast, explicitly draws the lifecycle looping back into Business Understanding, and ties that loop to concrete artefacts: updated project charters, retrained model versions. The difference suggests CRISP-DM, written in 1996 for data-mining projects that often ended at a delivered analysis or report, didn't anticipate that "the model runs continuously in production and needs to be revisited" would become the normal case. TDSP, written in the cloud/MLOps era, treats the loop-back as the expected steady state of a live system, not an edge case.
